items.stem: Define the term “changing ambitions”, and give one example.
items.answer: The shift in girls’ aspirations away from marriage and motherhood towards careers. Example: girls planning professional careers.

items.stem: Distinguish between “role model” and “coursework”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Role model: a person whose behaviour others copy (e.g. female teachers and head teachers). Coursework: assessed work completed during a course rather than in a final exam (e.g. a project counting towards the final grade).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Santiago, girls now outnumber boys at university by three to two, and more girls than boys achieve top grades at school. Suggest how a radical feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Radical feminism: despite girls’ success, education remains patriarchal: girls face sexual harassment, subject stereotyping and a curriculum and leadership dominated by men.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In Accra, girls now outnumber boys at university by three to two, and more girls than boys achieve top grades at school. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research boys’ attitudes to school work.
items.answer: Strengths: closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying boys’ attitudes to school work but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows exam results by gender for 400 pupils in Singapore. Table: percentage achieving five good passes at age 16 | 2000 | 2025. Girls | 51% | 62%. Boys | 50% | 61%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Boys between 2000 and 2025. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that boys are underachieving in education.
items.answer: (a) 61 − 50 = +11 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Girls, Boys; Girls had the highest figure for 2025. Feminism and changing ambitions have raised girls’ motivation (Sharpe). Qualifications: Both boys’ and girls’ results have improved; the gap may reflect girls improving faster rather than boys failing; class and ethnicity have larger effects than gender. The data also come from official statistics of 400 pupils aged 16 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 50 and 61; 1 mark for +11 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of self-completion questionnaires for studying why girls avoid physics and computer science.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why girls avoid physics and computer science but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into gender and subject choice, using official statistics with 1200 students aged 17-18 in Dhaka. Table: percentage of each gender taking the subject | Boys | Girls. Physics | 26% | 10%. Psychology | 16% | 32%. Computing | 21% | 13%. (a) Calculate the difference between Psychology and Computing for Boys and for Girls, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that subject choice is still strongly shaped by gender.
items.answer: (a) Boys: 5 percentage points; Girls: 19 percentage points; the difference is larger for Girls. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Girls than for Boys among Psychology; the figure is lower for Girls than for Boys among Physics, Computing; Psychology had the highest figure for Girls. Gender domains and early socialisation (Browne and Ross). Qualifications: Differences may have narrowed over time; individual choice and interest also matter; the data do not show reasons for choices. The data also come from official statistics of 1200 students aged 17-18 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (5 and 19); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful participant observation is for studying why girls avoid physics and computer science.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; by joining the group the researcher can gain verstehen and see the world through members’ eyes. Limitations: the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt; studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying why girls avoid physics and computer science but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying masculinity in a secondary school.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying masculinity in a secondary school but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. items.stem: Ethan is planning a study of boys’ attitudes to school work. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; one variable can be altered (for example the name on a job application) to test its effect. Limitations: the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory; they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying boys’ attitudes to school work but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).

items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying gender differences in exam results.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying gender differences in exam results but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes a person’s sense of themselves as masculine or feminine?
items.answer: Gender identity
items.markingKey: Gender identity: a person’s sense of themselves as masculine or feminine. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “gender identity”.
items.answer: A person’s sense of themselves as masculine or feminine.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a person’s sense of themselves as masculine or feminine. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “verbal abuse” and “gender identity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Verbal abuse: name-calling used to police gender and sexual identities (e.g. calling a boy who likes dance “gay”). Gender identity: a person’s sense of themselves as masculine or feminine (e.g. a girl avoiding subjects she sees as “for boys”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In a school in Madrid, 80% of pupils taking computer science are boys, while 75% of those taking health and social care are girls. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: gendered subject choice results from socialisation, stereotyped images and careers advice, which schools can change through equal opportunities policies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Lucas, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on gender and subject choice in Bangkok. The report was based on 240 students aged 17-18. Table: percentage of each gender taking the subject | Boys | Girls. Physics | 26% | 14%. Psychology | 10% | 30%. Computing | 25% | 14%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Boys and Girls for Physics (Girls minus Boys)?
items.answer: -12 percentage points
items.markingKey: 14 − 26 = -12 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Freya, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on gender and subject choice in Singapore. The report was based on 800 students aged 17-18. Table: percentage of each gender taking the subject | Boys | Girls. Physics | 29% | 16%. Psychology | 18% | 29%. Computing | 25% | 15%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for Girls. (b) Calculate the difference between Physics and Psychology for Boys and for Girls, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (c) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of gender and subject choice.
items.answer: (a) Psychology (29%). (b) Boys: 11 percentage points; Girls: 13 percentage points; the difference is larger for Girls. (c) Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public.
items.markingKey: (a) Psychology, 29%. [1] (b) 1 mark each difference (11 and 13); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (c) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2]

items.stem: The table shows results from research into gender and subject choice, using official statistics with 600 students aged 17-18 in Colombo. Table: percentage of each gender taking the subject | Boys | Girls. Physics | 24% | 13%. Psychology | 14% | 31%. Computing | 21% | 13%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Boys and Girls for Physics. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of gender and subject choice. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that subject choice is still strongly shaped by gender.
items.answer: (a) 13 − 24 = -11 percentage points (Girls compared with Boys). (b) They are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Girls than for Boys among Psychology; the figure is lower for Girls than for Boys among Physics, Computing; Psychology had the highest figure for Girls. Gender domains and early socialisation (Browne and Ross). Qualifications: Differences may have narrowed over time; individual choice and interest also matter; the data do not show reasons for choices. The data also come from official statistics of 600 students aged 17-18 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 24 and 13; 1 mark for 11 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the dominant form of masculinity, associated with toughness, heterosexuality and power?
items.answer: Hegemonic masculinity
items.markingKey: Hegemonic masculinity: the dominant form of masculinity, associated with toughness, heterosexuality and power. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Epstein meant by arguing that working-class boys are harassed and labelled “gay” if they appear to work hard.
items.answer: Epstein found working-class boys who worked hard were labelled “swots” or “gay”, so many avoided being seen to work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Epstein found working-class boys who worked hard were labelled “swots” or “gay”, so many avoided being seen to work. [2]

items.stem: Francis argued that laddish behaviour is a way for boys to protect their masculine status. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Francis found boys more concerned than girls about being labelled as swots, and laddishness was linked to popularity. Criticism: Laddish behaviour is also found among some girls (“ladettes”).
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Liberal feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Zara, a sociology student, is designing a project on boys’ attitudes to revision. Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of boys’ attitudes to revision. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying masculinity in a secondary school.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying masculinity in a secondary school but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]
